summary: Apogee is a browser-based mission-design game where players plan, build and fly a complete space mission. They choose a destination (Earth, the Moon and Mars at first, with Venus through Neptune, Mercury and the Sun unlocked through career mode), pick an orbit and a launcher, then assemble a spacecraft part by part: engines, tanks, power, antennas and instruments. Six live resource budgets (mass, power, cost, data, comms and time) show margins in real time. A design review checks concept maturity against NASA/JPL-style reserve rules, and a deterministic launch simulation resolves the flight with no dice, so the same design always flies the same way. A post-mission debrief explains what worked and why. Apogee turns real systems-engineering ideas (margins, trade-offs, the rocket equation) into something anyone can learn by playing. Every kilogram is a decision.
details:
What it does

Apogee is a browser-based game where players design and fly an entire space mission, rather than simply build a rocket.

Players select a destination and mission objective, choose an orbit and launch vehicle, and assemble a spacecraft from individual components. Six live resource budgets — mass, power, budget, data, communications and time — help players understand how decisions in one subsystem affect the rest of the mission.

The engineering dashboard also evaluates supporting parameters such as delta-v, battery capacity and ion propulsion power. Before launch, a design review checks spacecraft readiness, resource margins and mission requirements.

Players can then fly the mission using autopilot or manually perform departure and orbit-insertion burns for additional science return. A deterministic flight simulation resolves the mission, followed by a debrief explaining the outcome, science return, engineering failures and possible improvements.

How NASA data drives it

1. Live space weather — NASA DONKI

Apogee fetches the previous 30 days of solar flare and coronal mass ejection (CME) data from NASA's DONKI API.

The peak recorded solar-flare class determines a radiation multiplier:

  • Nominal: 0.96
  • Elevated: 1.05
  • Severe: 1.15

This multiplier influences projected spacecraft operational life in radiation-exposed orbits and the severity of the game's scripted solar-flare event when triggered, affecting science return. Solar-flare and CME counts are also tracked and displayed.

The game does not replay individual real-world DONKI events as individual mission events. Instead, it uses recent NASA space-weather observations to influence its simplified radiation environment.

If the API is unavailable, Apogee falls back to an offline baseline and clearly labels the data source as "Offline sample", allowing the game to continue functioning.

2. Planetary data — NASA Planetary Fact Sheets

Apogee uses NASA's Planetary Fact Sheets and individual planetary, Moon and Sun fact sheets to populate destination briefings. These provide reference information such as planetary gravity, temperatures, atmospheric composition, day and year lengths, and moons and rings.

NASA's mean distance-from-Sun values are also used to derive relative solar-flux factors for seven planets: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Using the inverse-square relationship:

Solar flux relative to Earth = (Earth's mean Sun distance / destination's mean Sun distance)²

These derived factors influence the solar power available to spacecraft at different destinations.

Earth and Moon use normalized gameplay values, while the Sun's solar-flux value is a simplified placeholder for its scripted mission-failure scenario.

3. NASA/JPL engineering frameworks

Apogee adapts established systems-engineering guidance into gameplay mechanics:

  • 10% reserve (Easy Mode): Based on the budget-reserve recommendation in NASA's CubeSat 101 guide.
  • 35% margin (Hard Mode): Inspired by the JPL Concept Maturity Level 4 technical-margin guidance for spacecraft dry mass, power and energy.
  • 80% design-review threshold: Inspired by the nominal checklist-completion guidance in the JPL Concept Maturity Level framework.

These are simplified gameplay policies, not universal NASA requirements for every spacecraft resource. NASA's systems-engineering webinar, Design and Develop Science Missions, also helped shape the mission-design process.

Honest numbers

Every numerical value in the game-data layer carries source and verification metadata. NASA-derived values identify their source and, where applicable, the derivation used. Other values are explicitly marked "simplified for gameplay" or "unverified" rather than being presented as real-world engineering specifications.

Apogee is an educational engineering simulation, not a flight-qualified spacecraft-design tool.

Why it's different

  • Complete mission design: Players manage an entire spacecraft and its subsystems, not just its launch vehicle.
  • Visible engineering trade-offs: Changes to spacecraft components affect the six core resource budgets and supporting engineering checks in real time.
  • NASA data integration: Live space-weather observations and NASA-derived planetary data influence game calculations and destination information.
  • Hands-on flight: Players can manually perform departure and orbit-insertion burns for up to 6% additional science return combined, or use autopilot.
  • Deterministic simulation: The same spacecraft design, simulation seed, weather inputs and manual-burn precision produce the same flight outcome.
  • Career progression: Completing missions unlocks progressively more challenging destinations across the Solar System, including Venus, Mercury and the outer planets.
  • A physics-based challenge: The Sun mission is deliberately impossible, demonstrating the difficulty of reaching the Sun from Earth using the simplified mission model.
  • Shareable designs: Players can share and load spacecraft designs using a design code.
  • Fast onboarding: Quick Demo and Try a Failing Design provide ready-made spacecraft configurations, allowing first-time visitors to experience mission outcomes and debriefs without building a spacecraft from scratch.

Built with

Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript using native ES modules and Canvas. No frameworks, npm dependencies or build step. Hosted on Vercel.

AI use

AI tools assisted the team with parts of implementation and presentation:

  • Code: Gemini, Claude and ChatGPT assisted with writing, debugging and refining code.
  • Text: AI assistance was used to write and edit project documentation and in-game text.
  • Visual assets: AI assistance was used to create some visual design assets.
  • AI-generated music: "Misty Echoes of Neptune" and "Interstellar Jazz Adventure" were generated through StockTune.

AI-assisted source files identify the tools used and include human-review acknowledgements. The concept, mission scenarios and overall design decisions belong to the team.
